subject: Business
title: Mirroring: The Simplest Trust Builder
description: A micro-lesson that makes Mirroring: The Simplest Trust Builder usable.

hook.text: An FBI hostage negotiator repeats the last three words of a kidnapper's sentence. The kidnapper opens up.

buildup.text: Mirroring means repeating key words or phrases. It makes people feel heard without you saying much.

discovery.text: Chris Voss used this in hostage situations. It buys time, builds rapport, and draws out information.

twist.text: It feels too simple to work. But studies show mirroring increases tips for waiters by 70%.

climax.text: In business, mirroring slows aggressive negotiators. They hear their own words and soften their stance.

punchline.text: Repeat their words. They'll keep talking.

quiz.question: Why is mirroring effective in negotiations?
options: It makes people feel heard and encourages them to share more

details.summary: Mirroring in negotiation means repeating the last few words someone said, which encourages them to elaborate, builds rapport, and makes them feel heard. Chris Voss identifies mirroring as the simplest and most effective tool for building trust and gathering information quickly.
details.whyItMatters: Mirroring requires almost no skill to execute but delivers outsized results. It keeps the other party talking, reveals information, and creates a sense of connection. FBI negotiators use it as their primary tool in critical hostage situations.
takeaways: Repeat the other person's last few words to encourage elaboration naturally
Mirroring builds rapport by making the speaker feel genuinely heard and understood
Chris Voss considers it the simplest high-impact technique for any negotiation

faq.question: How do you mirror effectively without sounding like a parrot?
faq.answer: Repeat only the last one to three critical words with a slightly upward intonation. Then pause and let silence work. The other person naturally feels the need to elaborate. Use it sparingly among other active listening techniques. The pause after mirroring is more important than the repetition.

faq.question: Why does such a simple technique work so well?
faq.answer: Humans are wired to clarify when they feel incompletely understood. Mirroring signals listening without revealing your position. It slows the conversation, giving you time to think. It builds subconscious rapport because we naturally like people who seem to understand us.
